Keplerian orbital elements at an epoch: semi-major axis (au), eccentricity, inclination (deg), mean anomaly (deg), argument of periapsis (deg), and longitude of ascending node (deg). Used as input to planetary/moon position calculations.
Time-derivative rates of the Keplerian elements, typically per century. Used to propagate orbital elements from a reference epoch.
Additional coefficients used by the ephemeris model for planetary positions (exact roles depend on model; typically periodic correction terms).

Header record for the Yale Bright Star Catalog 5. Contains catalog-wide metadata such as star range (STAR0/STAR1/STARN), total star count (STNUM), whether proper motions are present (MPROP), number of magnitudes (NMAG), and number of entries (NBENT). Exact semantics are inferred from field names; details not documented here.

One parsed BSC5 catalog entry. Fields include identifier/index (XNO), position at epoch (SRA0 right ascension, SDEC0 declination), a two-character spectral/class or flag field (IS), apparent magnitude (MAG), and proper motion components (XRPM, XDPM). Some field meanings inferred from names and may be incomplete.

Configuration for rendering behavior and runtime options (location, time, thresholds, toggles). Intended to be filled by caller and read by rendering logic. No constructors provided here; fields should be set directly.

Represents a star with sky position, proper motion, magnitude, catalog number, and shared render state in base.
Represents a planet with orbital elements/rates/extras references and magnitude plus shared render state. The Kep* types are referenced but defined elsewhere.
Represents the Moon with references to orbital elements and rates, magnitude, and shared render state.
Constellation line data: number of line segments and an array of star catalog numbers used to draw connections. Memory for star_numbers is managed by table-generation/free helpers.
Holds a star’s display name string. Arrays index by catalog number - 1.

Referenced planet structure used to hold per-planet data such as azimuth and altitude. Not defined in this header; definition likely resides in core.h or another header. Details unknown here.

Opaque-ish timestamp container that stores a time capture in a platform-appropriate representation. The val union holds one of: Windows LARGE_INTEGER (tick_win, only on _WIN32), an unsigned long long tick_apple (likely mach absolute time for Apple), POSIX struct timespec, or struct timeval. The val_member enum records which union field was most recently set to aid sanity checks. Intended for use with sw_gettime, sw_timediff_usec, and sw_sleep. Construction and population are performed by sw_gettime; users should not manually mix members across platforms.

Opaque-ish data record representing a city's name and its geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude). The struct contains a string pointer to the city name and two floats for latitude and longitude. Ownership and lifetime are managed by the API: obtain via get_city and release via free_city.
Pointer-to-pointer type implied by the field CityData::city_name. This is not a custom type defined in the header; ignoring per instructions.

functions.name: byte_to_char
functions.signature: char byte_to_char(uint8_t byte);

requirements: Argument byte may be any uint8_t value (0–255).
Callers should be aware that if char is signed on the target platform, values > 127 may convert to negative char values; interpretation is implementation-defined.
No errors are reported; the function always returns a char result.

buffer must point to at least 2 readable bytes.
Input bytes are expected to be in little-endian order (least significant byte first).
No bounds checking or error reporting is implied; caller must ensure buffer validity.

functions.signature: uint32_t bytes_to_uint32_LE(const uint8_t *buffer);
functions.description: Interprets the first four bytes at buffer as a little-endian 32-bit unsigned integer and returns the resulting uint32_t.

No bounds checking or error reporting is implied; caller must ensure buffer validity.

requirements: buffer must be non-null.
buffer must point to at least 4 readable bytes.
Input bytes are expected to be in little-endian order (least significant byte first).
No bounds checking or error reporting is implied; caller must ensure buffer validity.
Behavior for NaN/Inf payloads depends on platform floating-point representation (assumed IEEE-754 but not explicitly stated).

buffer must point to at least 8 readable bytes.

No bounds checking or error reporting is implied; caller must ensure buffer validity.
Behavior for NaN/Inf payloads depends on platform floating-point representation (assumed IEEE-754 but not explicitly stated).

requirements: buffer must be non-null.
buffer must point to at least 4 readable bytes.
Input bytes are expected to be in little-endian order (least significant byte first).
No bounds checking or error reporting is implied; caller must ensure buffer validity.
The precise rule for translating the 32-bit value to bool is unknown from the header; callers should expect conventional semantics (0 -> false, nonzero -> true) but this is not guaranteed.

functions.name: strptime
functions.signature: char *strptime(const char *s, const char *format, struct tm *tm);
functions.description: Parses the input date/time string s according to the strptime-style format string format and writes the parsed components into the struct tm pointed to by tm. On success, returns a pointer to the first character in s not consumed during parsing; on failure, returns NULL. Typical usage is to convert human-readable date/time text to a broken-down time structure for further processing (e.g., mktime). Behavior of textual fields (month/day names, AM/PM, timezones) is locale-dependent. Fields not specified by the format are generally left unmodified, so callers commonly initialize tm to a known state before calling. This header declares strptime when the platform lacks it (guarded by HAS_STRPTIME).
requirements: s must be a valid, null-terminated C string containing a date/time representation matching format.
format must be a valid, null-terminated strptime format string using recognized conversion specifiers (e.g., %Y, %m, %d, %H, %M, %S).
tm must be non-null and point to writable memory for a struct tm; the function writes parsed fields into this struct.
If the caller relies on values for fields not parsed by format, it should initialize tm to a known state before calling (unspecified fields may be left unchanged).
The caller must check the return value: NULL indicates parsing failed; a non-NULL return points to the first unparsed character in s.
Values in s corresponding to format directives must be within valid ranges for those directives (e.g., months 1–12, hours 0–23), otherwise parsing may fail.
Parsing of names and locale-specific text is locale-dependent; ensure the desired C locale is set prior to calling if such fields are used.

functions.name: greenwich_mean_sidereal_time_rad
functions.signature: double greenwich_mean_sidereal_time_rad(double julian_date);
functions.description: Computes the Greenwich Mean Sidereal Time (GMST) in radians for a given Julian date. Intended for astronomical coordinate transformations and time computations. Note: comments indicate some angles may need normalizing; exact time scale for the input JD (e.g., UT1/UTC) is not specified.
requirements: julian_date must be a finite Julian Date number.
Returned angle is in radians; caller may need to normalize to [0, 2π) if required by downstream usage.
Exact time scale for julian_date is unknown from the header; use consistently with the implementation.

functions.name: datetime_to_julian_date
functions.signature: double datetime_to_julian_date(const struct tm *time);
functions.description: Converts a calendar date/time to a Julian Date as a double. Useful for feeding time into astronomical calculations.
requirements: time must be a non-null pointer to a valid, initialized struct tm.
Time zone/time scale (UTC vs local) is not specified; behavior depends on implementation.
The provided struct tm fields should represent a valid civil date/time.

functions.name: julian_date_to_datetime
functions.signature: struct tm julian_date_to_datetime(double julian_date);
functions.description: Converts a Julian Date to a civil calendar date/time, returned as a struct tm by value. Useful for presenting results in calendar form.
requirements: julian_date must be a finite Julian Date number within the supported range of struct tm.
Output time scale (UTC/local) is not specified in the header; treat as unknown.

functions.name: current_julian_date
functions.signature: double current_julian_date(void);
functions.description: Returns the current system time as a Julian Date. Convenience wrapper around system clock to obtain JD for "now".
requirements: Relies on system clock; accuracy and time scale are implementation-dependent.

functions.name: calc_star_position
functions.signature: void calc_star_position(double right_ascension, double ra_motion, double declination, double dec_motion, double julian_date, double *ITRF_right_ascension, double *ITRF_declination);
functions.description: Computes the relative/apparent position of a star at a given Julian date, outputting right ascension and declination in the terrestrial frame (ITRF). Intended to apply proper motion and Earth rotation effects to catalog positions.
requirements: ITRF_right_ascension must be a non-null pointer to receive output.
ITRF_declination must be a non-null pointer to receive output.
right_ascension and declination must be finite; their units are not specified in the header (radians vs degrees unknown).
ra_motion and dec_motion units are not specified (e.g., per year); caller must match the implementation’s expected units.
julian_date must be a finite Julian Date number.

functions.name: calc_planet_helio_ICRF
functions.signature: void calc_planet_helio_ICRF(const struct KepElems *elements, const struct KepRates *rates, const struct KepExtra *extras, double julian_date, double *xh, double *yh, double *zh);
functions.description: Computes the heliocentric ICRF rectangular equatorial coordinates of a planet (or the Sun) for a given Julian date using Keplerian elements and rates, plus any extra terms.
requirements: elements must be a non-null pointer; fields use units documented in the header (a in au; I, M, w, O in degrees; e unitless).
rates must be a non-null pointer; units documented in the header (da in au/century; dI, dM, dw, dO in deg/century).
extras must be a non-null pointer; meanings of b, c, s, f are not documented here (treated as unknown).
xh, yh, zh must be non-null pointers to receive output coordinates.
julian_date must be a finite Julian Date number.
Output coordinate units and frame are ICRF rectangular equatorial; distance units are not explicitly stated but typically match input a (likely au).

functions.name: calc_planet_geo_ICRF
functions.signature: void calc_planet_geo_ICRF(double xe, double ye, double ze, const struct KepElems *planet_elements, const struct KepRates *planet_rates, const struct KepExtra *planet_extras, double julian_date, double *xg, double *yg, double *zg);
functions.description: Computes the planet’s geocentric ICRF rectangular equatorial coordinates for a given Julian date. Uses the planet’s orbital elements and rates, and the provided (xe, ye, ze) reference position (likely Earth’s heliocentric ICRF position) to transform to a geocentric frame.
requirements: planet_elements must be a non-null pointer; units per header (a in au; I, M, w, O in degrees; e unitless).
planet_rates must be a non-null pointer; units per header (da in au/century; angular rates in deg/century).
planet_extras must be a non-null pointer; meanings of b, c, s, f are not documented here (unknown).
xg, yg, zg must be non-null pointers to receive geocentric output coordinates.

xe, ye, ze must be finite and in the same frame/units as used internally; the header implies these are rectangular ICRF coordinates (interpretation such as Earth heliocentric is inferred and not guaranteed).
julian_date must be a finite Julian Date number.

functions.name: calc_moon_geo_ICRF
functions.signature: void calc_moon_geo_ICRF(const struct KepElems *moon_elements, const struct KepRates *moon_rates, double julian_date, double *xg, double *yg, double *zg);
functions.description: Computes the Moon’s geocentric ICRF rectangular equatorial coordinates at a given Julian date from lunar elements and rates.
requirements: moon_elements must be a non-null pointer; units per header (a in au; I, M, w, O in degrees; e unitless).
moon_rates must be a non-null pointer; units per header (da in au/century; angular rates in deg/century).
xg, yg, zg must be non-null pointers to receive output coordinates.
julian_date must be a finite Julian Date number.
Distance units for outputs are not explicitly stated but typically match the semi-major axis input units (likely au).

functions.name: earth_rotation_angle_rad
functions.signature: double earth_rotation_angle_rad(double jd);
functions.description: Computes the Earth Rotation Angle (ERA) in radians for a given Julian date. ERA is the angle from the celestial intermediate origin to the terrestrial intermediate origin and is a replacement for Greenwich sidereal time (not the obliquity).
requirements: jd must be a finite Julian Date number.
Returned angle is in radians; caller may need to normalize to [0, 2π) depending on use.

functions.name: julian_to_gregorian
functions.signature: void julian_to_gregorian(double jd, int *year, int *month, int *day);
functions.description: Converts a Julian Date to a Gregorian calendar date (year, month, day). Outputs components via pointer arguments.
requirements: year must be a non-null pointer.
month must be a non-null pointer.
day must be a non-null pointer.
jd must be a finite Julian Date number.
Output month/day ranges follow Gregorian calendar; exact handling around calendar reform and fractional days is not specified in the header.

functions.name: get_zodiac_sign
functions.signature: const char *get_zodiac_sign(int month, int day);
functions.description: Returns the textual zodiac sign name corresponding to the provided month and day in the Gregorian calendar.
requirements: month and day should form a valid Gregorian date. Behavior for out-of-range values is unspecified in the header.

functions.name: get_zodiac_symbol
functions.signature: const char *get_zodiac_symbol(int month, int day);
functions.description: Returns a zodiac symbol (e.g., Unicode glyph) corresponding to the provided month and day in the Gregorian calendar.
requirements: month and day should form a valid Gregorian date. Behavior for out-of-range values is unspecified in the header.

functions.name: calc_moon_age
functions.signature: double calc_moon_age(double julian_date);
functions.description: Computes the normalized age of the Moon within the synodic month: age ∈ [0, 1], where 0 is New Moon and 0.5 is Full Moon.
requirements: julian_date must be a finite Julian Date number.
Return value is expected to be within [0, 1] per the header comment.

functions.name: moon_age_to_phase
functions.signature: enum MoonPhase moon_age_to_phase(double age);
functions.description: Maps a Moon age within the synodic month to a discrete MoonPhase enum (e.g., New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon).
requirements: age must be within [0, 1] as stated in the header comments.
Behavior for values outside [0, 1] is unspecified.

functions.name: get_moon_phase_name
functions.signature: const char *get_moon_phase_name(enum MoonPhase phase);
functions.description: Returns a descriptive string (e.g., "Full Moon", "Waxing Crescent") for the provided MoonPhase enum value.
requirements: phase must be a valid value of enum MoonPhase.

functions.name: get_moon_phase_image
functions.signature: const char *get_moon_phase_image(enum MoonPhase phase, bool northern);
functions.description: Returns an emoji or symbolic image representing the Moon’s phase. The northern parameter indicates hemisphere orientation (true for northern hemisphere, false otherwise).
requirements: phase must be a valid value of enum MoonPhase.
northern should be set to true for northern hemisphere orientation, false for southern; exact visual mapping is implementation-defined.

functions.name: decimal_to_dms
functions.signature: void decimal_to_dms(double decimal_value, int *degrees, int *minutes, double *seconds);
functions.description: Converts a decimal angle value to degrees–minutes–seconds components, writing the results to the provided output pointers.
requirements: degrees must be a non-null pointer.
minutes must be a non-null pointer.
seconds must be a non-null pointer.
decimal_value must be finite.
Exact interpretation of decimal_value units (e.g., decimal degrees) is not stated; assumed to be an angle.

functions.name: parse_entries
functions.signature: bool parse_entries(uint8_t *data, size_t data_size, struct Entry **entries_out, unsigned int *num_entries_out);
functions.description: Parses a Yale Bright Star Catalog 5 (BSC5) data buffer and produces an array of Entry records sorted by increasing catalog number (the default order in BSC5). The function allocates the output array and writes its pointer and the number of parsed entries to the provided output parameters. Returns false on error (e.g., file/data error). Typical usage: load the BSC5 file into memory, pass its pointer and size, and receive an allocated array of Entry along with its count to iterate over. The caller is responsible for freeing the allocated array when done.
requirements: data must point to a valid memory buffer containing the BSC5 file contents and remain valid for the duration of the call.
data_size must be the size in bytes of the buffer referenced by data and accurately reflect the buffer length.
entries_out must be a non-null pointer to a struct Entry* variable to receive the allocated array pointer.
num_entries_out must be a non-null pointer to an unsigned int variable to receive the number of entries parsed.

On success, *entries_out points to heap-allocated memory that must be freed by the caller when no longer needed (freeing mechanism not specified; use the appropriate deallocator for the allocation used by this library).
On failure (function returns false), the contents of entries_out and num_entries_out are unspecified; callers should not use any partially written outputs unless the function returns true.
The resulting array is sorted by increasing catalog number as per BSC5 default ordering.

functions.name: equatorial_to_horizontal
functions.signature: void equatorial_to_horizontal(double right_ascension, double declination, double gmst, double latitude, double longitude, double *azimuth, double *altitude);
functions.description: Converts global equatorial coordinates (right ascension, declination) to local horizontal coordinates (azimuth, altitude), given observer location (latitude, longitude) and GMST. All angles are in radians and follow the conventions documented in this header (astronomical definitions; azimuth measured East of North, altitude measured from the equator to the zenith). Use to transform celestial positions for an observer at a given place/time.
requirements: All angle parameters (right_ascension, declination, gmst, latitude, longitude) are in radians, following the documented conventions.
azimuth and altitude must be valid, non-null pointers to receive results.
Caller should provide observer latitude and longitude consistent with the documented geographic conventions (longitude positive East, latitude positive North).
Function does not return a status code; caller should ensure inputs are meaningful for the intended observation (e.g., consistent epoch/time via gmst).

functions.name: equatorial_rectangular_to_spherical
functions.signature: void equatorial_rectangular_to_spherical(double xeq, double yeq, double zeq, double *right_ascension, double *declination);
functions.description: Converts rectangular equatorial coordinates (xeq, yeq, zeq) to spherical equatorial coordinates (right ascension, declination). All angles are in radians per the documented conventions. Use when you have a Cartesian direction vector in the equatorial frame and need RA/Dec.
requirements: right_ascension and declination must be valid, non-null pointers to receive results.
Input vector (xeq, yeq, zeq) should not be the zero vector to define a direction (inferred from spherical conversion).
Output angles are in radians and follow the documented equatorial conventions (RA measured East of the Vernal Equinox, declination measured North of the celestial equator).

functions.name: horizontal_to_spherical
functions.signature: void horizontal_to_spherical(double azimuth, double altitude, double *theta_sphere, double *phi_sphere);
functions.description: Converts horizontal coordinates (azimuth, altitude) to spherical coordinates (theta, phi) as defined in this header. Angles are in radians; azimuth is measured East of North; altitude is measured from the equator to the zenith (complement of spherical phi). Use to move from local horizontal to the generic spherical parameterization used elsewhere.
requirements: All angles are in radians per the documented conventions.
theta_sphere and phi_sphere must be valid, non-null pointers to receive results.
Inputs azimuth and altitude should follow the documented horizontal definitions (azimuth East of North; altitude from equator to zenith).

functions.name: project_stereographic
functions.signature: void project_stereographic(double sphere_radius, double point_theta, double point_phi, double center_theta, double center_phi, double *radius_polar, double *theta_polar);
functions.description: Performs a generalized stereographic projection of a point on a sphere to the plane orthogonal to the radius at a chosen focus (center) point. Inputs are spherical angles for the point and for the projection center; output is polar coordinates (r, θ) on the projection plane. All angles are in radians per the documented conventions.
requirements: sphere_radius should be positive to represent a valid sphere radius (inferred from geometric meaning).
Angles (point_theta, point_phi, center_theta, center_phi) are in radians using the spherical conventions documented here (θ measured North of East; Φ is angular distance from +z).
radius_polar and theta_polar must be valid, non-null pointers to receive results.

functions.name: project_stereographic_south
functions.signature: void project_stereographic_south(double radius_sphere, double theta_sphere, double phi_sphere, double *r_polar, double *theta_polar);
functions.description: Stereographic projection of a spherical point onto the equatorial plane with the projection centered on the south pole (focus at the south pole). Outputs polar coordinates on the plane. All angles are in radians per the documented conventions. Note: The resulting point lies within the equatorial orthodrome (circle of radius R) only if −π/2 < Φ < π/2 (as documented).
requirements: radius_sphere should be positive to represent a valid sphere radius (inferred from geometric meaning).
Angles (theta_sphere, phi_sphere) are in radians using the spherical conventions documented here.
r_polar and theta_polar must be valid, non-null pointers to receive results.

functions.name: project_stereographic_north
functions.signature: void project_stereographic_north(double radius_sphere, double theta_sphere, double phi_sphere, double *r_polar, double *theta_polar);
functions.description: Stereographic projection of a spherical point onto the equatorial plane with the projection centered on the north pole (focus at the north pole). Outputs polar coordinates on the plane. All angles are in radians per the documented conventions. Note: The resulting point lies within the equatorial orthodrome (circle of radius R) only if π/2 < Φ < 3π/2 (as documented).
requirements: radius_sphere should be positive to represent a valid sphere radius (inferred from geometric meaning).
Angles (theta_sphere, phi_sphere) are in radians using the spherical conventions documented here.
r_polar and theta_polar must be valid, non-null pointers to receive results.

functions.name: polar_to_win
functions.signature: void polar_to_win(double r, double theta, int win_height, int win_width, int *row, int *col);
functions.description: Maps a point given in polar coordinates (r, θ) on the unit circle to integer screen space coordinates (row, col) for a window of given height and width. Angles are in radians per the documented conventions. Use to plot projected polar coordinates on a raster grid.
requirements: r is intended for the unit circle; callers should provide 0 <= r <= 1 to remain within the unit disk (inferred from description).
theta is in radians.
win_height and win_width should be positive integers representing the window dimensions (inferred from typical screen mapping).

import random
import datetime
import string

# We generate human-readable date/time strings that match one of several
# strptime-compatible format patterns used by the fuzzer stub. The output
# is a bytes buffer that the fuzzer will use via FUZZ_PARAM_STR/FUZZ_PARAM_FILENAME.
#
# Covered formats (matching the stub’s choices):
# 0: "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"
# 1: "%d/%m/%Y"
# 2: "%Y %j" (day-of-year, zero-padded to 3 digits)
# 3: "%b %d %Y %I:%M:%S %p" (C locale month abbrev)
# 4: "%a, %d %b %Y %H:%M:%S" (C locale weekday abbrev)
# 5: "%m/%d/%y %H:%M"
#
# We also optionally append a short trailing token (space + word) so that
# strptime may stop before the end to exercise return-pointer behavior.

MON_ABBR = ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"]
WDAY_ABBR = ["Sun","Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat"]

# Helper to zero-pad integers

def z(n, width):
    s = str(n)
    if len(s) < width:
        return "0" * (width - len(s)) + s
    return s

# Compute a valid yday for a given year

def max_yday(year: int) -> int:
    # Leap year check for proleptic Gregorian
    return 366 if (year % 400 == 0 or (year % 4 == 0 and year % 100 != 0)) else 365

# Construct a random trailing token to exercise partial-consume paths

def make_trailer(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    if rng.random() < 0.6:
        # 60% chance to add a trailer
        # Keep it short (<= 16 chars) and simple ASCII
        length = rng.randint(1, 12)
        alphabet = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + "_-"
        tok = ''.join(rng.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(length))
        return " " + tok
    return ""

# Generate a valid calendar date/time in safe ranges

def gen_components(rng: random.Random):
    # Year 1900..2199 as stub does
    year = 1900 + rng.randrange(0, 300)
    # Month/day/time in safe ranges
    mon = rng.randrange(1, 13)
    # Pick a valid day for that month/year
    if mon in (1,3,5,7,8,10,12):
        max_day = 31
    elif mon in (4,6,9,11):
        max_day = 30
    else:
        # February: check leap year
        max_day = 29 if max_yday(year) == 366 else 28
    mday = rng.randrange(1, max_day + 1)

    hour24 = rng.randrange(0, 24)
    minute = rng.randrange(0, 60)
    # Allow 0..60 to include potential leap second as stub permits
    second = rng.randrange(0, 61)

    # For 12-hour / AM-PM formats
    hour12 = (hour24 % 12)
    if hour12 == 0:
        hour12 = 12
    ampm = "AM" if rng.randrange(0, 2) == 0 else "PM"

    # Day-of-year within valid range for the chosen year
    yday = rng.randrange(1, max_yday(year) + 1)

    # Weekday index 0..6 for Sun..Sat (used only textually)
    wday = rng.randrange(0, 7)

    return {
        "year": year,
        "mon": mon,
        "mday": mday,
        "hour24": hour24,
        "minute": minute,
        "second": second,
        "hour12": hour12,
        "ampm": ampm,
        "yday": yday,
        "wday": wday,
    }

# Build a concrete string for a chosen format index 0..5

def build_for_format(fi: int, c: dict) -> str:
    if fi == 0:
        # %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S
        return (
            f"{c['year']}-" + z(c['mon'],2) + "-" + z(c['mday'],2) +
            " " + z(c['hour24'],2) + ":" + z(c['minute'],2) + ":" + z(c['second'],2)
        )
    elif fi == 1:
        # %d/%m/%Y
        return z(c['mday'],2) + "/" + z(c['mon'],2) + "/" + str(c['year'])
    elif fi == 2:
        # %Y %j (j is zero-padded to 3)
        return f"{c['year']} " + z(c['yday'],3)
    elif fi == 3:
        # %b %d %Y %I:%M:%S %p
        mon_ab = MON_ABBR[c['mon'] - 1]
        return (
            f"{mon_ab} " + z(c['mday'],2) + f" {c['year']} " +
            z(c['hour12'],2) + ":" + z(c['minute'],2) + ":" + z(c['second'],2) +
            f" {c['ampm']}"
        )
    elif fi == 4:
        # %a, %d %b %Y %H:%M:%S
        wday_ab = WDAY_ABBR[c['wday']]
        mon_ab = MON_ABBR[c['mon'] - 1]
        return (
            f"{wday_ab}, " + z(c['mday'],2) + f" {mon_ab} {c['year']} " +
            z(c['hour24'],2) + ":" + z(c['minute'],2) + ":" + z(c['second'],2)
        )
    else:
        # %m/%d/%y %H:%M
        y2 = c['year'] % 100
        return (
            z(c['mon'],2) + "/" + z(c['mday'],2) + "/" + z(y2,2) +
            " " + z(c['hour24'],2) + ":" + z(c['minute'],2)
        )

# Public API

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Pick a format index resembling the stub’s selection space
    fi = rng.randrange(0, 6)

    c = gen_components(rng)
    s = build_for_format(fi, c)

    # Append optional trailer to exercise partial-consume behavior
    s += make_trailer(rng)

    # Ensure we stay under 4096 bytes
    if len(s) > 4096:
        s = s[:4096]

    return s.encode("ascii")

import random
import struct
import datetime

# We generate buffers intended to seed FUZZ_PARAM_STR used for the input string (s)
# in the strptime fuzzer stub. The stub synthesizes both format and matching s,
# but it may also append a trailing string from FUZZ_PARAM_STR. We provide valid,
# interesting trailing data that exercises partial-consume behavior without breaking parsing.
# We also sometimes return a complete date-time string by itself so that, if the harness
# uses this data as a filename or another FUZZ_PARAM_STR earlier, it still looks valid.

FMT_VARIANTS = [
    ("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", "iso"),
    ("%d/%m/%Y", "euro"),
    ("%Y %j", "yday"),
    ("%b %d %Y %I:%M:%S %p", "mon_ampm"),
    ("%a, %d %b %Y %H:%M:%S", "rfc_no_tz"),
    ("%m/%d/%y %H:%M", "us_short"),
]

MON_ABBR = ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"]
WDAY_ABBR = ["Sun","Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat"]


def clamp(v, lo, hi):
    return lo if v < lo else hi if v > hi else v


def synth_one(format_key, rng):
    # Produce a date string matching the selected format and a trailing token.
    # Respect ranges used by the fuzzer stub: years 1900..2199, mday 1..28 safe, allow leap second 60.
    year = 1900 + rng.randrange(0, 300)
    mon = 1 + rng.randrange(0, 12)
    mday = 1 + rng.randrange(0, 28)
    hour = rng.randrange(0, 24)
    minute = rng.randrange(0, 60)
    # Occasionally use 60 to exercise leap-second allowance
    second = rng.choice([rng.randrange(0, 60), 60])
    yday = 1 + rng.randrange(0, 365)
    wday = rng.randrange(0, 7)
    hour12 = (hour % 12) or 12
    ampm = rng.choice(["AM", "PM"]) if hour12 else ("AM")

    if format_key == "iso":
        s = f"{year:04d}-{mon:02d}-{mday:02d} {hour:02d}:{minute:02d}:{second:02d}"
    elif format_key == "euro":
        s = f"{mday:02d}/{mon:02d}/{year:04d}"
    elif format_key == "yday":
        s = f"{year:04d} {yday:03d}"
    elif format_key == "mon_ampm":
        s = f"{MON_ABBR[mon-1]} {mday:02d} {year:04d} {hour12:02d}:{minute:02d}:{second:02d} {ampm}"
    elif format_key == "rfc_no_tz":
        s = f"{WDAY_ABBR[wday]}, {mday:02d} {MON_ABBR[mon-1]} {year:04d} {hour:02d}:{minute:02d}:{second:02d}"
    elif format_key == "us_short":
        s = f"{mon:02d}/{mday:02d}/{year%100:02d} {hour:02d}:{minute:02d}"
    else:
        # Fallback iso
        s = f"{year:04d}-{mon:02d}-{mday:02d} {hour:02d}:{minute:02d}:{second:02d}"

    # Generate a trailing token that is valid-yet-extra to exercise end pointer behavior.
    # Keep short to limit size.
    trails = [
        "Z",                        # common trailing marker
        "UTC",                      # timezone-like
        "extra",                    # generic text
        "note123",                  # alnum
        "+0100",                    # RFC offset-like
        "(comment)",                # braced text
        "μs",                       # UTF-8 bytes exercise
        "#tag",                     # symbol prefix
        "TAIL",                     # uppercase
        "END"                        # sentinel
    ]
    trail = rng.choice(trails)
    # 50% include trailing, 50% empty
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        s = f"{s} {trail}"
    return s


def gen_trailing_blob(rng, max_len=64):
    # Construct a varied trailing blob that remains parse-friendly if appended after a space.
    # Include ASCII, digits, punctuation, and some UTF-8 sequences.
    parts = []
    vocab = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789_-:/.,#()[]"
    # Random length 1..max_len
    n = rng.randint(8, max_len)
    while len("".join(parts)) < n:
        choice = rng.random()
        if choice < 0.75:
            k = rng.randint(1, 8)
            parts.append("".join(rng.choice(vocab) for _ in range(k)))
        elif choice < 0.9:
            # UTF-8 snippet
            parts.append(rng.choice(["µ", "°", "Ω", "✓", "Δ", "π"]))
        else:
            # Number or offset-like
            parts.append(rng.choice(["+0000", "+0530", "-0700", "Z", "UTC"]))
        if len(parts) > 16:
            break
    blob = " ".join(parts)
    return blob[:max_len]


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    # Decide content mode:
    #  - 0: Provide only a short trailing string (used by FUZZ_PARAM_STR at the end)
    #  - 1: Provide a valid complete date-time string matching one format
    #  - 2: Provide a valid date-time string plus a richer trailing blob
    mode = rng.choices([0, 1, 2], weights=[2, 4, 4], k=1)[0]

    fmt, key = rng.choice(FMT_VARIANTS)
    s = synth_one(key, rng)

    if mode == 0:
        out = gen_trailing_blob(rng, max_len=32)
    elif mode == 1:
        out = s
    else:
        out = s + " " + gen_trailing_blob(rng, max_len=48)

    # Ensure size bound
    if len(out) > 4096:
        out = out[:4096]

    return out.encode("utf-8", errors="ignore")

import random
import struct
from typing import List

# We construct a plausible fixed-size binary record sequence for BSC5 entries.
# Layout mapped to struct Entry fields (little-endian):
#   XNO   : float32
#   SRA0  : float64
#   SDEC0 : float64
#   IS    : 2 bytes
#   MAG   : float32
#   XRPM  : float64
#   XDPM  : float32
# This yields 4 + 8 + 8 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 38 bytes per record.
# Keep buffer size <= 2048 (stub cap) and <= 4096.

_RECORD_FMT = '<fdd2sfdf'
_RECORD_SIZE = struct.calcsize(_RECORD_FMT)

_RA_RAD_MIN, _RA_RAD_MAX = 0.0, 2.0 * 3.141592653589793
_DEC_RAD_MIN, _DEC_RAD_MAX = -0.5 * 3.141592653589793, 0.5 * 3.141592653589793
_MAG_MIN, _MAG_MAX = -1.5, 12.0
_PM_RA_MIN, _PM_RA_MAX = -0.1, 0.1
_PM_DEC_MIN, _PM_DEC_MAX = -0.1, 0.1

def _rand_is_field(rng: random.Random) -> bytes:
    # Two-character field; use ASCII letters/digits and sometimes spaces.
    alphabet = b"ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ0123456789  "
    return bytes([rng.choice(alphabet), rng.choice(alphabet)])

def _gen_entry(rng: random.Random, xno: int) -> bytes:
    ra = rng.uniform(_RA_RAD_MIN, _RA_RAD_MAX)
    dec = rng.uniform(_DEC_RAD_MIN, _DEC_RAD_MAX)
    is2 = _rand_is_field(rng)
    mag = rng.uniform(_MAG_MIN, _MAG_MAX)
    xrpm = rng.uniform(_PM_RA_MIN, _PM_RA_MAX)
    xdpm = rng.uniform(_PM_DEC_MIN, _PM_DEC_MAX)
    xno_f = float(xno)
    return struct.pack(_RECORD_FMT, xno_f, ra, dec, is2, mag, xrpm, xdpm)

def _choose_num_records(rng: random.Random) -> int:
    max_rec = max(1, 2048 // _RECORD_SIZE)
    if max_rec <= 3:
        return max_rec
    a = rng.randint(1, max_rec)
    b = rng.randint(1, max_rec)
    return max(1, min(max_rec, (a + b) // 2))

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    nrec = _choose_num_records(rng)
    entries: List[bytes] = []
    catalog = 1
    for _ in range(nrec):
        entries.append(_gen_entry(rng, catalog))
        catalog += 1 if rng.random() < 0.85 else rng.randint(2, 5)
    data = b''.join(entries)
    # Ensure we don't exceed the stub's cap and keep whole records only
    if len(data) > 2048:
        full = (2048 // _RECORD_SIZE) * _RECORD_SIZE
        data = data[:full]
    return data

    # simple weighted selection
    total = sum(weights)
    x = rng.random() * total
    acc = 0.0
    for item, w in zip(items, weights):
        acc += w
        if x <= acc:
            return item
    return items[-1]


def _star_name_variants(rng: random.Random, cat_num: int) -> List[str]:
    variants = []
    # Proper name alone
    variants.append(_rand_weighted_choice(rng, PROPER_NAMES))
    # Bayer with constellation
    variants.append(f"{_rand_weighted_choice(rng, BAYER_DESIGNATIONS)} {_rand_weighted_choice(rng, CONSTELLATIONS)}")
    # Greek letter with constellation
    variants.append(f"{_rand_weighted_choice(rng, UNICODE_NAME_FRAGMENTS)} {_rand_weighted_choice(rng, CONSTELLATIONS)}")
    # Catalog-like aliases
    variants.append(f"HR {cat_num}")
    variants.append(f"HD {cat_num * 5 + 1}")
    variants.append(f"SAO {100000 + (cat_num % 99999)}")
    # Mixed with hyphen/apostrophe/space
    base = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, PROPER_NAMES)
    deco = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, ["'", "-", " ", "  ", ""], [0.2, 0.2, 0.4, 0.1, 0.1])
    tail = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, ["A", "B", "C", "I", "II", "III", "IV", "V"]) if deco else ""
    variants.append((base + deco + tail).strip())
    # Unicode sprinkle
    if rng.random() < 0.7:
        uni = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, UNICODE_NAME_FRAGMENTS)
        variants.append(f"{base} {uni}")
    return variants


def _format_line(rng: random.Random, idx: int, name: str) -> str:
    sep = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, SEPARATORS, [0.45, 0.25, 0.2, 0.1])
    if sep == ",":
        # maybe CSV-quote the name
        if rng.random() < 0.6 or ("," in name) or ('"' in name):
            # escape quotes by doubling
            qname = '"' + name.replace('"', '""') + '"'
        else:
            qname = name
        return f"{idx},{qname}\n"
    else:
        return f"{idx}{sep}{name}\n"


def _gen_comment_line(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    prefix = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, COMMENT_PREFIX)
    content_opts = [
        " BSC5 Names", " Mapping file", " Generated", " Unicode OK", " Version 1",
    ]
    # occasional empty comment
    if rng.random() < 0.2:
        return prefix + "\n"
    return prefix + _rand_weighted_choice(rng, content_opts) + "\n"


def _gen_blank_line(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    # Mix of truly blank and whitespace-only lines
    if rng.random() < 0.5:
        return "\n"
    ws = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, [" ", "\t", "  ", "\t \t"]) 
    return ws + "\n"


def _unique_indices(rng: random.Random, count: int, min_idx: int, max_idx: int) -> List[int]:
    # ensure uniqueness and spread
    possible = list(range(min_idx, max_idx + 1))
    rng.shuffle(possible)
    return possible[:max(0, min(count, len(possible)))]


def _build_lines(rng: random.Random, target_bytes: int) -> str:
    lines: List[str] = []

    # Header comments
    if rng.random() < 0.9:
        for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3)):
            lines.append(_gen_comment_line(rng))

    # Random blank lines sprinkled
    if rng.random() < 0.6:
        lines.append(_gen_blank_line(rng))

    # Decide approximate number of mapping lines
    # Keep modest to stay under 4KB; names can be long with Unicode
    n_lines = rng.randint(20, 200)

    # Choose index span; typical BSC5 has ~9k stars with HR numbers; use 1..10000 span
    min_idx = 1
    max_idx = rng.choice([1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 10000])

    # Unique indices, but we will also introduce some duplicates intentionally
    idxs = _unique_indices(rng, n_lines, min_idx, max_idx)

    for i, idx in enumerate(idxs):
        # Select a name variant
        name = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, _star_name_variants(rng, idx))
        # Occasionally add alternate names after a delimiter (parser may pick first token or whole rest)
        if rng.random() < 0.25:
            alt = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, _star_name_variants(rng, idx))
            joiner = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, [" | ", "; ", " / ", ", "])
            name = name + joiner + alt
        # Occasionally append constellation in parentheses
        if rng.random() < 0.3:
            name += f" ({_rand_weighted_choice(rng, CONSTELLATIONS)})"
        lines.append(_format_line(rng, idx, name))
        # Inject duplicates for edge behavior: repeat same index with different formatting or name
        if rng.random() < 0.1:
            alt_name = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, _star_name_variants(rng, idx))
            lines.append(_format_line(rng, idx, alt_name))
        # Sprinkle comments or blanks between entries
        r = rng.random()
        if r < 0.05:
            lines.append(_gen_comment_line(rng))
        elif r < 0.1:
            lines.append(_gen_blank_line(rng))

    # Add some boundary/edge indices explicitly (1, max, large gaps)
    for special_idx in [1, max_idx, max(2, max_idx - 1)]:
        if rng.random() < 0.7:
            name = _rand_weighted_choice(rng, _star_name_variants(rng, special_idx))
            lines.append(_format_line(rng, special_idx, name))

    # Ensure final newline and clip to size
    text = "".join(lines)
    if not text.endswith("\n"):
        text += "\n"

    # Trim carefully to <= MAX_BYTES while keeping last char newline
    if len(text) > MAX_BYTES:
        text = text[:MAX_BYTES]
        if not text.endswith("\n"):
            # back up to last newline if possible; else force one
            last_nl = text.rfind("\n")
            if last_nl != -1:
                text = text[: last_nl + 1]
            else:
                text = text[:-1] + "\n"
    return text


def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    # Small randomness beyond seed for variability between calls with same seed in same process could be added,
    # but requirement states results should be seeded and random each time given a seed; we stick to deterministic.

    text = _build_lines(rng, MAX_BYTES)

    # Encode as UTF-8; parser likely treats input as bytes; ensure valid encoding
    data = text.encode('utf-8', errors='strict')
    # Safety cap
    if len(data) > MAX_BYTES:
        data = data[:MAX_BYTES]
        # Ensure trailing newline
        if not data.endswith(b"\n"):
            data = data.rstrip(b"\r\n") + b"\n"
    return data

import random
from typing import List

def _rand_between(rng: random.Random, a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return rng.randint(a, b)

# We do not know exact grammar of bsc5_constellations.txt, but typical formats use
# lines of star-number pairs (or sequences) separated by spaces/commas and comments.
# We'll generate a conservative, valid-looking ASCII text that ends with a newline
# and exercises a variety of layouts:
# - comment lines starting with '#'
# - blank lines
# - pairs "n1 n2" (space separated)
# - pairs "n1,n2" (comma separated)
# - longer polylines like "n1 n2 n3 n4" to allow parser to split into segments
# - constellation headers like 
#     [CONSTELLATION NAME]
#     n1 n2; n2 n3; n3 n4
# - mixed whitespace, tabs, multiple spaces
# - large and small catalog numbers within a plausible range (1..1_000_000)
# - optional inline comments after data
# - ensure final newline
# This aims to be accepted by a tolerant parser while exploring different code paths.

def _make_star_num(rng: random.Random) -> int:
    # Bias towards smaller numbers but allow large ones
    modes = [
        lambda: _rand_between(rng, 1, 500),
        lambda: _rand_between(rng, 501, 5000),
        lambda: _rand_between(rng, 5001, 50000),
        lambda: _rand_between(rng, 1, 120000),
    ]
    return rng.choice(modes)()

def _pair_line_space(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    a, b = _make_star_num(rng), _make_star_num(rng)
    sep = rng.choice([" ", "\t", "    "])
    return f"{a}{sep}{b}\n"

def _pair_line_comma(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    a, b = _make_star_num(rng), _make_star_num(rng)
    sep_ws = rng.choice(["", " ", "\t"])  # allow spaces around comma
    return f"{a}{sep_ws},{sep_ws}{b}\n"

def _polyline_space(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    count = _rand_between(rng, 3, 8)
    nums = [str(_make_star_num(rng)) for _ in range(count)]
    # random spacing
    pieces: List[str] = []
    for i, n in enumerate(nums):
        pieces.append(n)
        if i != count - 1:
            pieces.append(rng.choice([" ", "  ", "\t"]))
    return "".join(pieces) + "\n"

def _semicolon_pairs(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    # Produce "a b; c d; e f" style
    pair_cnt = _rand_between(rng, 2, 6)
    pairs = []
    for _ in range(pair_cnt):
        a, b = _make_star_num(rng), _make_star_num(rng)
        sep = rng.choice([" ", "\t"])
        pairs.append(f"{a}{sep}{b}")
    sep2 = rng.choice(["; ", ";\t", "; "])
    return sep2.join(pairs) + "\n"

def _constellation_block(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    names = [
        "Orion", "Ursa Major", "Scorpius", "Cassiopeia", "Cygnus",
        "Lyra", "Aquila", "Taurus", "Leo", "Virgo", "Sagittarius",
    ]
    header_style = rng.choice([
        lambda n: f"[{n}]\n",
        lambda n: f"## {n}\n",
        lambda n: f"Constellation: {n}\n",
    ])
    name = rng.choice(names)
    block = [header_style(name)]
    # followed by a few data lines
    for _ in range(_rand_between(rng, 2, 6)):
        line = rng.choice([
            _pair_line_space,
            _pair_line_comma,
            _polyline_space,
            _semicolon_pairs,
        ])(rng)
        # occasionally append inline comment
        if rng.random() < 0.25:
            comment = rng.choice([" # link", " // edge", " ; trail"])
            # insert comment before trailing newline
            line = line.rstrip("\n") + comment + "\n"
        block.append(line)
    return "".join(block)

def _comment_line(rng: random.Random) -> str:
    prefix = rng.choice(["#", "//", ";", "%"])  # common comment tokens
    text = rng.choice([
        " Constellation lines", " Auto-generated", " BSC5 format", " data",
    ])
    return f"{prefix}{text}\n"

def _blank_line() -> str:
    return "\n"

def generate(seed: int) -> bytes:
    rng = random.Random(seed)

    lines: List[str] = []

    # Optional file prologue comment and metadata
    if rng.random() < 0.8:
        lines.append(_comment_line(rng))
    if rng.random() < 0.4:
        lines.append(_blank_line())

    # Emit several constellation blocks and interleave simple lines
    total_blocks = _rand_between(rng, 2, 6)
    for b in range(total_blocks):
        lines.append(_constellation_block(rng))
        # interleave with some simple lines
        for _ in range(_rand_between(rng, 1, 4)):
            gen = rng.choice([
                _pair_line_space,
                _pair_line_comma,
                _polyline_space,
                _semicolon_pairs,
                _comment_line,
                _blank_line,
            ])
            if gen in (_comment_line, _blank_line):
                lines.append(gen(rng) if gen is _comment_line else gen())
            else:
                lines.append(gen(rng))

    # Ensure file ends with newline and size limit
    text = "".join(lines)
    if not text.endswith("\n"):
        text += "\n"

    # Trim to 4096 bytes while preserving final newline
    if len(text) > 4096:
        text = text[:4095]
        if not text.endswith("\n"):
            text = text[:-1] + "\n"
    return text.encode("utf-8")
